vectors.enisa_quote: proximity operations where rogue space objects approach space assets
vectors.reason: ENISA names rogue space objects approaching the satellite and space- or ground-based weapons acting on it; both are the proximity origin (a close vehicle or a counterspace weapon node).

rows.reason: Concealment and decoys are not mentioned; ENISA says rogue objects approach but not that they hide.
Blending into a debris field is a stealth posture that ENISA does not describe.
Observing or perturbing physical byproducts of computation extracts secrets; ENISA's spying is capability assessment, not side-channel attack.

rows.enisa_quote: Deliberate physical damage to the satellite or some of its segments
rows.sparta_quote: The adversary inflicts damage by physically striking space assets
rows.reason: Physical destruction of the satellite by a kinetic strike is the outcome ENISA states.
rows.role_reason: EX-0017 is a SPARTA Execution technique, but the physical destruction by an ASAT is the outcome ENISA states, so it closes the chain as impact

rows.enisa_quote: space or ground based directed nergy weapons or kinetic weapons
rows.sparta_quote: launching from the Earth to damage or destroy a satellite in orbit
rows.reason: Ground-launched kinetic ASAT is described.
A rogue space object ramming the satellite is the co-orbital ASAT.

rows.enisa_quote: Deliberate physical damage to the satellite or some of its segments
rows.sparta_quote: The adversary inflicts physical effects on a satellite without mechanical contact
rows.reason: Physical damage by directed energy without contact is the outcome ENISA states for energy weapons.
rows.role_reason: EX-0018 is a SPARTA Execution technique, but physical damage by energy weapons is the outcome ENISA states, so it closes the chain as impact

rows.sparta_quote: An EMP delivers a broadband, high-amplitude electromagnetic transient
rows.reason: ENISA names EMP and high-altitude nuclear detonation.

rows.enisa_quote: high-powered laser weapons, laser dazzling and blinding
rows.sparta_quote: If directed toward a satellite’s optical center, the attack is known as blinding or dazzling
rows.reason: ENISA names high-powered laser weapons, dazzling and blinding.

rows.sparta_quote: High-powered microwave (HPM) weapons can be used to disrupt or destroy a satellite’s electronics
rows.reason: ENISA names high-powered microwave weapons.
Side-channel exfiltration infers secrets from physical byproducts; ENISA names no secret extraction.
Power analysis needs measurement of the target's own power draw; not stated for an approaching object.
Electromagnetic-leakage analysis is a signal-analysis method; the ENISA text states only spying in general, which EXF-0005 covers.
Traffic analysis of relays and constellations is not described by the ASAT text.
Timing attacks on responses are not described.
Thermal imaging of processors is not described.

rows.enisa_quote: for the purpose of assessing their capabilities (spying)
rows.sparta_quote: A nearby vehicle serves as the collection platform for unintended emissions
rows.reason: Proximity spying on the satellite is stated as a purpose of the approach.
Insertion of malicious code or data during manufacturing or delivery is the supply-chain compromise of TR55; ASAT damage is not delivered through a supplier.
Poisoning developer dependencies and build tools is a supply-chain method (TR55); no software is mentioned in TR18.
Altering software before delivery is supply-chain compromise (TR55); no delivery step in the ASAT text.
Altering boards or programmable logic before delivery is the built-in tainted hardware of TR15, not an ASAT attack.
Compromising a software-defined radio is a radio-side foothold; not part of the weapons or proximity operations that ENISA lists.
A compromised neighbour satellite over an inter-satellite link is not a rogue object in the ENISA sense; no crosslink is described.
A secondary communication path is not mentioned in the ASAT description.
A backup ground station is not mentioned; the ground element of TR18 is a weapon, not a station foothold.
The backup RF receive path is not mentioned in the ASAT description.

rows.sparta_quote: co-orbit and approach a target closely enough for local sensing, signaling, or physical interaction
rows.reason: A rogue space object reaches the satellite by rendezvous and proximity operations before spying or ramming; it is the entry of the co-orbital ramming step (single-valued enables; the spying entry is IA-0005.01).

rows.sparta_quote: an adversary analyzes unintentional emissions to infer sensitive information
rows.reason: ENISA says the approach is 'for the purpose of assessing their capabilities (spying)'; observing emissions from a local vantage point is how a nearby object assesses a spacecraft, and EXF-0005 (kept) is the same activity, so the entry that leads to it is kept.
Docking or OSAM capture is a connection of another vehicle (TR20 'docking of another satellite'), not an ASAT strike.
ENISA says 'physical contact (ramming)': the parenthesis defines contact as a collision, while grappling captures the target to reach ports and debug pads; the text does not describe capture.
A hosted payload as a door into the bus is not mentioned; the ASAT text does not describe an interface.
Compromising the mission ground system is a cyber foothold; TR18 describes weapons and approaching objects.
Tampering with the update pipeline is not part of an ASAT attack as ENISA describes it.
Commanding through a valid ground station is not an ASAT attack; no commanding is described.
Rogue External Entity is an actor-controlled transmitter interacting over RF to gain a foothold; ENISA's rogue objects act physically or with weapons.
A rogue ground station transmitting mission signals is not what TR18 describes; its ground-based weapons are directed-energy or kinetic.
Rogue Spacecraft in SPARTA is a local RF peer emitting or relaying signals; ENISA's rogue objects spy, ram or fire weapons.

rows.sparta_quote: directed-energy systems can dazzle sensors or upset electronics
rows.reason: The counterspace weapon is the node that delivers the directed-energy or kinetic attack from space or ground.
A trusted relationship is not mentioned in the ASAT description.
Mission collaborators as access route are not mentioned in TR18.
Vendor access is a supply-chain relationship (TR55); no vendor appears in TR18.
End-user equipment as attacker origin is not mentioned in the ASAT description.
Timing first execution to safe-mode is not described; the ASAT effects are physical.
Tainted peripherals and removable media are the rogue hardware/software connection of TR20, not an ASAT attack.
Compromise of assembly, test and launch operations is a pre-launch cyber compromise; the ASAT text has no ground-test setting.
The host spacecraft as a door into a hosted payload is not mentioned in TR18.
Using functions that already exist is not destruction by an ASAT weapon.
Forcing a state or mode change is the unauthorized-guidance-command behaviour of TR28, not weapon damage.
Altering settings while the code remains intact is parameter modification (TR57), not physical damage.
Falsifying or deleting data is data modification (TR39), not physical damage.
Blocking or redirecting commands and data is the traffic manipulation of TR32.
Replacing firmware or logic is firmware corruption (TR42), not physical damage.
Depleting a resource is resource exhaustion (TR51); ASAT damage is physical.
Altering the clock or synchronisation is not described by the ASAT text.
Pivoting from a hosted payload into the host is not described; an ASAT strike does not pivot.
Hopping between satellites over a crosslink is not described by TR18.
A visiting-vehicle interface used for lateral movement after docking is the docking scenario of TR20; ASAT proximity operations here do not connect to the target.
Close-range observation of the target is how the approach assesses capabilities (spying); it feeds the kept information gathering.
